extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public interested in morals, taste, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and literary essays (The Spectator) addressing subjects like dreams, the imagination, marriage, and reading; combines aesthetic theory, practical advice, and moral commentary for a general educated readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Gallants' submission to mistresses
rubrics_metrics.description: These Sort of Fellows ... swallow ill Usage from one to whom they have no Obligation, but from a base Passion, which it is mean to indulge, and which it would be glorious to overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral standard that men who submit to mistresses through mere passion are behaving meanly; overcoming base passion is presented as the noble course. Examples and anti-patterns: men who leave wealth to paramours or who are 'Cully in the Grave' are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of men leaving families for paramours
rubrics_metrics.description: They have carried on the Jest in the very Article of Death, and, to the Diminution of the Wealth and Happiness of their Families, ... have left immense Wealth to their Paramours. What is this but being a Cully in the Grave!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral standard about duty and reputation: abandoning family interests (e.g., bequeathing fortunes to mistresses) is portrayed as disgraceful and gullible; used as an example of extreme 'Cullyism'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams as evidence of the soul's activity and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams may give us some Idea of the great Excellency of an Human Soul, and some Intimation of its Independency on Matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative/aesthetic claim used as a criterion for judging the nature of the soul: because dreams display mental activity during sleep, they indicate the soul's vitality beyond bodily functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams demonstrate the mind's sustained activity when the body rests
rubrics_metrics.description: our Dreams are great Instances of that Activity which is natural to the human Soul, and which it is not in the power of Sleep to deaden or abate... the Soul exerts her self in her several Faculties, and continues in Action till her Partner is again qualified to bear her Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative criterion: even when the body is exhausted, mental faculties (invention, speech, imagination) remain active in dreams; examples include composing, speaking languages, and making unpremeditated harangues while asleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-invention: invention works with ease in dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not a more painful Action of the Mind, than Invention; yet in Dreams it works with that Ease and Activity, that we are not sensible when the Faculty is employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evidence that the mind's creative powers are more free in dreaming; supports claims about the soul's agility and the nature of imaginative production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions and devotion are heightened in dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: the Passions affect the Mind with greater Strength when we are asleep, than when we are awake. Joy and Sorrow give us more vigorous Sensations of Pain or Pleasure at this time... Devotion likewise ... is in a very particular manner heightned and inflamed, when it rises in the Soul at a time that the Body is thus laid at Rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological/aesthetic observation presented as general principle (with a nod to individual variation) and used to support philosophical problems about happiness in dreams versus waking life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams create a private world: the soul produces its own company
rubrics_metrics.description: She converses with numberless Beings of her own Creation, and is transported into ten thousand Scenes of her own raising. She is herself the Theatre, the Actors, and the Beholder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic/philosophical claim (supported by Plutarch/Heraclitus) used to argue for the soul's grandeur: during sleep the mind generates a multiplicity of ideas and private scenes, implying independence and creative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dreams as possible divine or spiritual communications
rubrics_metrics.description: That several such Divinations have been made, none can question ... Whether such dark Presages, such Visions of the Night proceed from any latent Power in the Soul ... or from any Communication with the Supreme Being, or from any operation of Subordinate Spirits, has been a great Dispute among the Learned; the matter of Fact is, I think, incontestable...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic/aetiological claim: dreams sometimes contain divinations; while causes are debated (soul power, God, spirits), historical and scriptural instances are presented as uncontestable facts supporting the possibility of revelatory dreams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soul remains partially connected to the body in dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not suppose, that the Soul in these Instances is entirely loose and unfettered from the Body: It is sufficient, if she is not so far sunk, and immersed in Matter ... The Corporeal Union is slackned enough to give the Mind more Play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced metaphysical claim: dreams show loosened but not severed body-soul union; supports intermediate position between full detachment and full embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: To achieve the sublime, gather circumstances that truly terrify the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Longinus ... recommends one in Homer ... because the Poet has not amused himself with little Fancies upon the occasion ... but because he has gathered together those Circumstances which are the most apt to terrify the Imagination, and which really happen in the raging of a Tempest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic guideline for writers/artists: avoid trivial or fanciful details in descriptions of grandeur; instead assemble authentic, terrifying particulars that correspond to real experience (example: storm at sea in Homer and Psalm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness of sensible objects produces pleasure and prompts metaphysical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness is one [source of the Pleasures of the Imagination] ... the Sea or Ocean ... gives his Imagination one of the highest kinds of Pleasure that can arise from Greatness... Such an Object naturally raises in my Thoughts the Idea of an Almighty Being, and convinces me of his Existence as much as a metaphysical Demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic/philosophical criterion: exposure to vast natural objects (sea/ocean) elicits sublime pleasure and leads the imagination/understanding to the idea of a transcendent creator; used as justification for certain poetic or pictorial subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice on affording periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: If my Readers will not go to the Price of buying my Papers by Retail, let them have Patience, and they may buy them in the Lump... if they retrench any the smallest Particular in their ordinary Expence, it will easily make up the Half Penny a Day...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consumer/pricing guidance directed at readers: economize small daily expenses (sacrifice a ribbon, burn one candle less) or purchase collected volumes to afford the paper; publisher's note on editions and gift suitability of volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage as an institution of mutual comfort and highest human felicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is an Institution calculated for a constant Scene of as much Delight as our Being is capable of... Two Persons who have chosen each other ... have in that Action bound themselves to be good-humour'd, affable, discreet, forgiving, patient and joyful, with respect to each other's Frailties and Perfections, to the End of their Lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and practical guidance for married conduct: spouses should cultivate amiability, discretion, patience, forgiveness, and friendship; true friendship between married persons produces a higher pleasure than initial fervour and is the basis of lasting happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading stories as moral exercise: preference for narratives where justice prevails
rubrics_metrics.description: The Writings that please me most ... are Stories, for the Truth of which there is good Authority. The Mind of Man is naturally a Lover of Justice, and when we read a Story wherein a Criminal is overtaken ... the Soul enjoys a certain Revenge for the Offence done to its Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary recommendation: choose well-authenticated stories that satisfy a natural appetite for justice; such narratives provide moral satisfaction and serve as food for the imagination when reading briefly between other labours.
